---
title: "The Fourier transform as a change of basis in $L^2$"
description: "A short note on viewing the Fourier transform not as a formula, but as a rotation between orthonormal bases of a function space."
date: 2025-07-24
categories: [mathematics, functional-analysis]
---

## Motivation

We usually meet the Fourier transform as a formula,

$$
\hat{f}(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, e^{-2\pi i x \xi}\, \mathrm{d}x ,
$$

but this hides the structural idea. The transform is better understood as a
**change of orthonormal basis** in the Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.

## Vectors and functions

In $\mathbb{R}^n$ a vector $\mathbf{v}$ is expanded in an orthonormal basis
$\{\mathbf{e}_k\}$ as

$$
\mathbf{v} = \sum_k \langle \mathbf{e}_k, \mathbf{v}\rangle\, \mathbf{e}_k .
$$

A function $f \in L^2$ behaves the same way, with the inner product

$$
\langle g, f\rangle = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \overline{g(x)}\, f(x)\, \mathrm{d}x .
$$

The complex exponentials $e_\xi(x) = e^{2\pi i x \xi}$ play the role of the
basis vectors $\mathbf{e}_k$. The Fourier coefficient $\hat{f}(\xi)$ is nothing
but the projection $\langle e_\xi, f\rangle$.

## Why this matters

Because the transform is a **unitary** map, it preserves inner products —
this is Parseval's theorem,

$$
\int |f(x)|^2\, \mathrm{d}x = \int |\hat{f}(\xi)|^2\, \mathrm{d}\xi ,
$$

which is simply the statement that a rotation of the basis does not change
the length of a vector.
